title: As costs climb, how can Denver restaurants keep customers coming back?
summary: We asked a food writer about the latest dining trends.
content: It’s no secret that the cost of eating out is going up. In the Denver area, it’s up 3.8 percent in the past year ending in September. Restaurant owners are also facing sticker shock when it comes to food and labor costs, so many are experimenting with ways to keep customers coming back, according to a recent article for the Denver Post. Here are some takeaways from Colorado Matters’ conversation with the article’s author, food and travel writer Patricia Kaowthumrong . Answers have been lightly edited for clarity. Restaurant owners are trying to keep prices as low as possible Kaowthumrong spoke with Cristian Anderson, who co-owns Chop Shop, a chain of several fast-casual restaurants. She said Anderson is prioritizing customer visits over profit right now. “The hope for some restaurant owners like Cristian Anderson is that if you focus on lowering prices, you can get more diners in and get some regulars by offering that value … It’s better than having empty seats,” Kaowthumrong told Colorado Matters. “When they’re taking a hit financially, it’s worth it because they’re still getting customers in their restaurants.” Owners are taking some of the pricier items off the menu At Denver restaurants, the cost to serve some menu items, like steak, is rising faster than others. Kaowthumrong said some owners like Anderson no longer serve certain dishes because they’ve found customers won’t pay higher prices. “In [Anderson’s] case, it was a very popular short rib dish but the ingredients were just so expensive that the menu price got so high that he decided, well, we can’t make it smaller because then customers will think it’s shrinkflation, but we can’t charge more because customers just can’t afford it, so we’ll just take it off the menu,” Kaowthumrong said. Restaurants are experimenting with take-out family meals to make eating out more affordable Especially in neighborhoods with a lot of families, restaurants are selling a 4-serving family option that costs less than four separate meals. “They’re trying to give customers the most value possible just so they’ll remember them and come in again,” Kaowthumrong said. “There’s a lot of things folks are doing just to gain some attention or compete more with other restaurants because there are so many trying to survive right now.” The concept of radical hospitality as a business model Taylor Herbert, one of the co-owners of the new restaurant Mother Other, believes “radical hospitality” is one way to engender loyalty among customers and employees alike, Kaowthumrong said. The restaurant, which is on South Broadway, is in a location without a lot of foot traffic, so people aren’t likely to walk by and just pop in. “They really have to make guests feel seen and appreciated when they come in. And that includes learning [customer] names and just making the entire experience wonderful for guests,” Kaowthumrong said. “It kind of starts with employees… being happy with their roles and feeling like part of this great ecosystem and then guests feel nurtured so they want to come back.” Some restaurants are cutting back hours to save on labor costs Restaurants might decide to close for an extra day during the week when fewer customers tend to dine out. Mother Other operates on a four-day work week. Some are eliminating certain meals that don’t draw a lot of customers. “If you see a restaurant remove brunch, it might be to save money on labor because they have to staff those meals and do prep and the whole shebang, and it is often cheaper to keep staff on certain schedules,” Kaowthumrong said. On what dining out options might look like in the future Kaowthumrong said ever since she became a food reporter eight years ago, she’s worried that the stress on restaurants will result in more restaurant closures and fewer options for dining out. But she thinks restaurants are generally resilient. “People still need a place to meet friends and have experiences outside the home,” Kaowthumrong said. “They’re just simply being more selective about where they go, how often and what feels the right expense. So I don’t think they’re going away by any means.”

title: A Chinese restaurant owner was feeding homeless people. Then the customers joined in
summary: A patron of Jade Cafe bought 100 meals for people in need. Others added dozens more.
content: Murals of animals cover the walls of Jade Cafe in southwest Denver, all hand-painted by owner Phu Nguyen. But he may be most proud of what’s displayed on a wall by the kitchen. The space is lined with dozens of receipts for orange chicken, fried rice and sesame chicken. Each slip of paper represents an act of kindness — a “pay-it-forward” meal purchased by customers for people in need. The receipts are adorned with words of encouragement like “You got this!” and “You are loved.” A wall covered in pay-it-forward meals at Jade Cafe in Denver’s Bear Valley neighborhood, purchased by customers for others in need. Nov. 18, 2026. The tradition was born earlier this year, when Nguyen started providing free meals for homeless people who came into his restaurant at 5600 W. Dartmouth Ave. Now, customers have stepped up to help, too. “The idea came from one of my customers. We have a homeless community here, and they’ve been stopping by and I’ve been feeding them. And this customer saw us and he asked if he could buy his next meal,” Nguyen said. “It seemed like a very good idea, so we decided to adopt it.” Nguyen and the wall’s first supporter, Roger, marked that first meal by taping the receipt to the wall. Soon came another and another, each person adding to this wall of supporters for those who need it most. Hannah Son, employee at Jade Cafe in Denver’s Bear Valley neighborhood, works the register during a lunch shift. Nov. 18, 2026. So many meals Prior to running his family’s restaurant, Nguyen worked as an artist and had part-time gigs at a pizza place and at Jade Cafe. He always wanted to help people, but he simply didn’t have the means. But when he took over Jade Cafe after his brother retired last year, he saw his chance. Almost a year after he took over, about 75 receipts are taped to the wall, which represent only a portion of this community act of giving. Some recipients stop in daily for food. Others don’t need the help for long: One person returned to thank Nguyen after they secured a job and apartment nearby. “We do have regular people come in and we feed on a daily basis,” Nguyen said. “The breadth of it isn’t too much, but we’re still able to affect the change of several people.” Nguyen said it’s a way to treat people with dignity when they’re down on their luck. “I’ve seen them sit in the rain and eat. I’ve seen them go back to the river behind us and eat and it makes a difference,” he said. “And I feel it, our employees feel it. It’s not often where you give people food and they start crying. I think it’s difficult for some people to ask, most people to ask.” Phu Nguyen, owner of Jade Cafe in Denver’s Bear Valley neighborhood, stands for a portrait in front of a mural he painted inside of the restaurant. Nov. 18, 2026. Around 40 people have funded the meals, Nguyen estimated. One customer, Kerry Bilewski, bought 100 meals herself, intended for people experiencing homelessness as well as local first responders. “When it came to my attention that this is something Phu was promoting for the community in Bear Valley, it was a no-brainer for me,” Bilewski wrote in an email. “The pay-it-forward program seemed an easy way to counteract this negativity since no matter who you are, where you come from, or what your socio-economic background is, we all need food to survive.” Nguyen plans to keep the wall running as long as he can. Hannah Son, employee at Jade Cafe in Denver’s Bear Valley neighborhood, serves lunch to customers during a lunch shift. Nov. 18, 2026. More than a restaurant Nguyen’s parents immigrated from China in 1980, then saved their money for years to open Jade Cafe in 1988. All the recipes come from Nguyen’s father and brother. His cousin, Yang Zhong, is the main chef in the back, stir-frying saucy meat in a wok that glows from a blue-and-gold fire. Yang Zhong, chef at Jade Cafe in Denver’s Bear Valley neighborhood, cooks fried rice during a lunch shift. Nov. 18, 2026. During my recent visit, coworkers laughed with each other in the kitchen. New customers greeted Nguyen, saying a friend recommended visiting. “We’re so proud of our community. It’s vibrant and the people are so nice,” he said. “People just become regular customers — and the ‘Hi,’ ‘Hello,’ becomes ‘Hey, how did you do in your test?’ or ‘How are your kids doing?’” Inside the restaurant, Nguyen displays an “Immigrant Kitchen” sign proudly below the cash register. He offers discounts for teachers and donates proceeds from his homemade chili oil to organizations that help domestic violence survivors and oppose Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Hannah Son, employee at Jade Cafe in Denver’s Bear Valley neighborhood, serves lunch to customers during a lunch shift. Nov. 18, 2026. “We want to remind people that when you’re getting Chinese food, it’s Chinese people who immigrated here, work their a** off,” he said. “We want to make a voice and be heard and actually make a difference.” To buy a meal for someone in need, simply stop by the restaurant.To buy a meal for someone in need, simply stop by the restaurant or order online for pickup and write “pay it forward” in the name option. Regular customers Khari Hobbs (from left), Amillie Merced and Demeakie Hobbs eat lunch at Jade Cafe in Denver’s Bear Valley neighborhood. Nov. 18, 2026.
